description: Sliding Window track: 4 lessons, 10 knowledge checks, 7 practice problems.

coding.title: Maximum Vowels in a Window
coding.problemStatement: Given a string of lowercase letters and a number k, find the largest number of vowels (`a`, `e`, `i`, `o`, `u`) in any substring of length exactly k.
coding.inputFormat: The first line contains the string s. The second line contains k.
coding.outputFormat: A single integer: the maximum number of vowels in a window of length k.

examples.explanation: There are no vowels at all.

referenceSolutions.PYTHON:
s = input().strip()
k = int(input())
vowels = set("aeiou")
count = sum(1 for ch in s[:k] if ch in vowels)
best = count
for i in range(k, len(s)):
    count += (s[i] in vowels) - (s[i - k] in vowels)   # one enters, one leaves
    best = max(best, count)
print(best)

coding.title: Count Anagram Windows
coding.problemStatement:
Given a text s and a pattern p, count the positions where a substring of s is an **anagram** of p — the same letters with the same counts, in any order.

Overlapping matches all count.
coding.inputFormat: The first line contains s. The second line contains p. Both use lowercase letters only.
coding.outputFormat: A single integer: the number of start positions i where s[i .. i + |p| - 1] is an anagram of p.

referenceSolutions.PYTHON:
s = input().strip()
p = input().strip()
m = len(p)
need = [0] * 26
have = [0] * 26
for ch in p:
    need[ord(ch) - 97] += 1
count = 0
for i, ch in enumerate(s):
    have[ord(ch) - 97] += 1              # letter entering the window
    if i >= m:
        have[ord(s[i - m]) - 97] -= 1    # letter leaving the window
    if i >= m - 1 and have == need:
        count += 1
print(count)

coding.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
coding.problemStatement: Given a string, find the length of the longest **substring** (contiguous) in which no character appears twice.
coding.inputFormat: A single line containing the string s (lowercase letters and digits).
coding.outputFormat: A single integer: the length of the longest substring with all-distinct characters.
constraints: s contains lowercase letters and digits only

examples.explanation: "abc" is the longest; any longer window repeats a letter.
"wke". Note "pwke" is not a substring — it skips a character.

referenceSolutions.PYTHON:
s = input().strip()
last = {}          # character -> index where it was last seen
left = best = 0
for right, ch in enumerate(s):
    if ch in last and last[ch] >= left:
        left = last[ch] + 1          # jump past the earlier copy
    last[ch] = right
    best = max(best, right - left + 1)
print(best)

coding.title: Longest Subarray with Sum at Most K
coding.problemStatement:
Given an array of **non-negative** integers and a number K, find the length of the longest contiguous subarray whose sum is at most K.

Print 0 if no single element is small enough.
coding.inputFormat: The first line contains n and K. The second line contains n non-negative integers.
coding.outputFormat: A single integer: the length of the longest subarray with sum <= K.

examples.explanation: Every element is already bigger than 5.

referenceSolutions.PYTHON:
n, k = map(int, input().split())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))
left = total = best = 0
for right in range(n):
    total += a[right]            # grow the window
    while total > k:             # shrink until it's valid again
        total -= a[left]
        left += 1
    best = max(best, right - left + 1)
print(best)

coding.title: Longest Substring with At Most K Distinct Characters
coding.problemStatement: Given a string and a number k, find the length of the longest substring that contains **at most k different characters**.
coding.inputFormat: The first line contains the string s (lowercase letters). The second line contains k.
coding.outputFormat: A single integer: the length of the longest valid substring.

examples.explanation: The whole string uses one character.

referenceSolutions.PYTHON:
s = input().strip()
k = int(input())
count = {}
left = best = 0
for right, ch in enumerate(s):
    count[ch] = count.get(ch, 0) + 1
    while len(count) > k:            # too many distinct: shrink from the left
        out = s[left]
        count[out] -= 1
        if count[out] == 0:
            del count[out]           # it no longer counts as distinct
        left += 1
    best = max(best, right - left + 1)
print(best)

coding.title: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
coding.problemStatement:
Given an array of **positive** integers and a target, find the length of the **shortest** contiguous subarray whose sum is at least the target.

Print 0 if even the whole array falls short.
coding.inputFormat: The first line contains n and target. The second line contains n positive integers.
coding.outputFormat: A single integer: the minimum length, or 0.

examples.explanation: [4, 3] sums to 7 with only two elements.

referenceSolutions.PYTHON:
n, target = map(int, input().split())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))
left = total = 0
best = n + 1
for right in range(n):
    total += a[right]
    while total >= target:        # valid: record it, then try to shrink
        best = min(best, right - left + 1)
        total -= a[left]
        left += 1
print(best if best <= n else 0)

coding.title: Subarrays with Product Less Than K
coding.problemStatement: Given an array of **positive** integers and a number k, count the contiguous subarrays whose product is **strictly less than** k.
coding.inputFormat: The first line contains n and k. The second line contains n positive integers.
coding.outputFormat: A single integer: the number of subarrays.

referenceSolutions.PYTHON:
n, k = map(int, input().split())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))
left = count = 0
product = 1
for right in range(n):
    product *= a[right]
    while product >= k and left <= right:
        product //= a[left]
        left += 1
    count += right - left + 1     # every window that ends at right and starts in [left, right]
print(count)

mcqs.title: Sliding Window check: updating a fixed window
mcqs.questionText: A window of length k slides one step to the right. What is the least work needed to update a count of vowels inside it?
mcqs.explanation: Consecutive windows share k − 1 characters; only one enters and one leaves. Adjusting for just those two makes every slide O(1) and the whole scan O(n).

options.optionText: Add 1 if the entering character is a vowel, subtract 1 if the leaving one is — O(1)
Recount the k characters of the new window — O(k)
Recount the whole string — O(n)
Sort the window and count — O(k log k)

mcqs.title: Sliding Window check: what to track for anagrams
mcqs.questionText: To check whether each length-|p| window of s is an anagram of p, what should the window keep up to date?
mcqs.explanation: Anagrams have equal letter counts, so keep 26 counters: +1 for the entering letter, −1 for the leaving one, then compare with p's counts. A sum of codes can collide ("ad" and "bc"), a set forgets counts, and re-sorting every window costs O(m log m).

options.optionText: A count for each letter in the window, compared with p's counts
The sum of the letters' codes
The window's letters in sorted order
The set of distinct letters in the window

mcqs.title: Sliding Window check: tracing a fixed window
mcqs.explanation: Windows of length 3: "abc" (1 vowel), "bci" (1), "cii" (2), "iii" (3), "iid" (2), "ide" (2), "def" (1). The maximum is 3.
mcqs.codeSnippet:
s, k = "abciiidef", 3
count = sum(ch in "aeiou" for ch in s[:k])
best = count
for i in range(k, len(s)):
    count += (s[i] in "aeiou") - (s[i - k] in "aeiou")
    best = max(best, count)
print(best)

mcqs.title: Sliding Window check: why left never moves back
mcqs.questionText: In a longest-valid-window scan, `left` only ever moves right. Why is the whole algorithm O(n) even though there is a loop inside a loop?
mcqs.explanation: Count pointer moves, not loop nesting: `right` moves n times, and `left` can't move more than n times over the whole run because it never goes back. So the total work is O(n) — this is called amortised analysis.

options.optionText: Each index enters the window once and leaves it at most once, so both pointers move at most n times in total
The inner loop runs at most once per step
Because the input is sorted
It isn't — the worst case is O(n²)

mcqs.title: Sliding Window check: longest without repeats
mcqs.explanation: "abba": the window grows to "ab" (2). The second b jumps left past the first b: window "b". Then a's last index is 0, which is before left, so it is ignored: window "ba" (2). Without the `>= left` check, the last a would move left back to 1, and the window "bba" — which repeats b — would be counted, giving a wrong 3.

mcqs.title: Sliding Window check: when a window can't be used
mcqs.questionText: You want the longest subarray with sum at most K, and the array contains **negative** numbers. Why does the grow-and-shrink window fail?
mcqs.explanation: The window relies on monotonicity: with non-negative values, dropping the leftmost element never increases the sum. A negative element breaks that. Use prefix sums instead (with a sorted structure or a hash map, depending on the question).

options.optionText: Removing an element from the left can make the sum larger, so shrinking no longer moves toward a valid window
Negative numbers can't be stored in the window
The window must then be of fixed size
It still works; only the answer's sign changes

mcqs.title: Sliding Window check: where to record the answer
mcqs.questionText: Finding the **shortest** window whose sum is at least the target, where should you record the answer?
mcqs.explanation: For the longest window you shrink until valid, then record. For the shortest you do the opposite: while the window is valid, record its length and try to shrink it further. Once it becomes invalid, it's too short, and you grow it again.

options.optionText: Inside the shrinking loop, each time the window is still valid
After the shrinking loop, once the window has become invalid
Only when right reaches the end of the array
Before adding a[right] to the window

mcqs.title: Sliding Window check: tracing the shortest window
mcqs.codeSnippet:
a, target = [2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 3], 7
left = total = 0
best = len(a) + 1
for right in range(len(a)):
    total += a[right]
    while total >= target:
        best = min(best, right - left + 1)
        total -= a[left]
        left += 1
print(best)

mcqs.title: Sliding Window check: counting windows per right end
mcqs.questionText: The valid window ending at `right` is `a[left..right]`, and every shorter window inside it is valid too. How many valid subarrays end at `right`?
mcqs.explanation: They start at left, left + 1, …, right — that's right − left + 1 subarrays. Adding this for every right counts all valid subarrays in O(n), without listing them.

options.optionText: right - left + 1
right - left
left + 1

mcqs.title: Sliding Window check: exactly K from at most K
mcqs.questionText: You can count subarrays with **at most** K distinct values using a window. How do you count those with **exactly** K?
mcqs.explanation: Every subarray with exactly K distinct values is counted by atMost(K) but not by atMost(K − 1); everything with fewer is counted by both and cancels. "Exactly" isn't monotone — adding an element can push you past K — but "at most" is, so turn one into two of the other.

options.optionText: atMost(K) − atMost(K − 1)
atMost(K) − 1
atMost(K + 1) − atMost(K)
atMost(K) / K

lessons.title: Fixed-size windows: tracking more than a sum
lessons.summary: Slide a window of length k and update whatever it tracks — counts, frequencies — in O(1) per step.
objectives: Maintain a window's state by handling only the element entering and the one leaving
Track letter counts in a window to detect anagrams
Initialise the first window correctly and slide from there
lessons.concept:
The Arrays track slid a fixed-length window to keep a running **sum**. The same idea works for anything you can update when one element enters and one leaves: a count of vowels, the frequency of each letter, the number of distinct values.

```python
# window state for s[0 .. k-1]
for i in range(k, len(s)):
    add(s[i])          # entering on the right
    remove(s[i - k])   # leaving on the left
    # the window is now s[i - k + 1 .. i]
```

Each slide is O(1) (or O(26) for letter counts), so all windows together cost O(n) — instead of O(n × k) to rebuild each one.

## Anagram windows

"Is this window an anagram of p?" means "does it have the same letter counts as p?" So keep an array of 26 counters for the window and one for p. When the window reaches length |p|, compare them; then slide. Comparing two arrays of 26 counts is constant work, so the scan is O(26 × n).

A refinement tracks how many of the 26 letters currently **match** p's count, and updates that number as counts change — then each step is truly O(1). The simple compare is plenty for most problems.
lessons.commonMistakes:
- **Checking before the first window is full.** Only compare once the window has reached length k (`i >= k - 1`).
- **Removing the wrong element.** When `s[i]` enters a window of length k, the one leaving is `s[i - k]`.
- **p longer than s.** Then no window exists — make sure the loop simply finds nothing rather than indexing out of range.
- **Rebuilding the counts for each window.** That's O(n × k) — update, don't recount.

lessons.title: Growing and shrinking: the longest valid window
lessons.summary: Extend the window on the right; when it breaks the rule, shrink it from the left until it's valid again.
objectives: Find the longest window satisfying a condition with a grow-and-shrink scan
Explain why the scan is O(n) despite the nested loop
Recognise when the technique needs the values to be non-negative
lessons.concept:
When the window's length isn't fixed, let the problem decide it. The **variable-size window** keeps two pointers, `left` and `right`:

1. Move `right` one step — the window grows by one element.
2. While the window **breaks the rule**, move `left` right — it shrinks.
3. Now the window is valid: record its length if it's the best so far.

```python
left = 0
for right in range(n):
    add(a[right])
    while not valid():
        remove(a[left])
        left += 1
    best = max(best, right - left + 1)
```

## Why it's O(n)

There's a loop inside a loop, but `left` never moves backwards. Over the whole run, `right` moves n times and `left` moves at most n times, so the total work is O(n).

## When it works

The rule must be **monotone**: if a window is valid, every smaller window inside it is valid too — and shrinking from the left always moves you toward validity. "Sum at most K" with **non-negative** numbers qualifies: dropping an element never raises the sum. With negative numbers it doesn't, and the window gives wrong answers — use prefix sums instead.

"No repeated characters" and "at most k distinct characters" are monotone too. For repeats there's a shortcut: remember where each character was last seen, and jump `left` straight past the earlier copy instead of shrinking one step at a time.
lessons.example:
Longest subarray with sum at most 5 in `[3, 1, 2, 1, 1, 4]`:

| right | add | total | shrink | window | length | best |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 3 | 3 | — | [3] | 1 | 1 |
| 1 | 1 | 4 | — | [3, 1] | 2 | 2 |
| 2 | 2 | 6 | drop 3 → 3 | [1, 2] | 2 | 2 |
| 3 | 1 | 4 | — | [1, 2, 1] | 3 | 3 |
| 4 | 1 | 5 | — | [1, 2, 1, 1] | 4 | **4** |
| 5 | 4 | 9 | drop 1, 2, 1 → 5 | [1, 4] | 2 | 4 |

At most k distinct characters, with a count per character:

```python
count = {}
left = best = 0
for right, ch in enumerate(s):
    count[ch] = count.get(ch, 0) + 1
    while len(count) > k:
        count[s[left]] -= 1
        if count[s[left]] == 0:
            del count[s[left]]
        left += 1
    best = max(best, right - left + 1)
```
lessons.commonMistakes:
- **Using the window with negative numbers.** Shrinking may not restore validity; the answer can be wrong without any error.
- **Recording the answer before the window is valid.** Shrink first, then record.
- **Leaving zero counts in the map.** A letter with count 0 isn't in the window; delete it, or `len(count)` overstates the distinct letters.
- **Letting `left` jump backwards.** With a last-seen map, only jump if the earlier copy is inside the window (`last[ch] >= left`).

lessons.title: The shortest window that works
lessons.summary: Flip the loop: grow until the window is valid, then shrink it while it stays valid, recording as you go.
objectives: Find the shortest window satisfying a condition
Place the answer update correctly for "shortest" versus "longest" problems
Handle the case where no window qualifies
lessons.concept:
"Longest valid window" and "shortest valid window" use the same two pointers with the inner loop turned around:

| Goal | Inner loop runs while the window is… | Record the answer… |
|---|---|---|
| Longest | **invalid** (shrink to fix it) | after the loop |
| Shortest | **valid** (shrink to improve it) | inside the loop |

For the shortest subarray with sum at least `target`:

```python
left = total = 0
best = n + 1                  # "not found yet"
for right in range(n):
    total += a[right]
    while total >= target:    # valid: record, then try smaller
        best = min(best, right - left + 1)
        total -= a[left]
        left += 1
print(best if best <= n else 0)
```

Every window you record is valid, and every time the window becomes invalid you've already recorded the shortest valid window ending at that `right`. Again each pointer moves at most n times: **O(n)**.

Monotonicity matters here as well: with **positive** numbers, adding elements only raises the sum and removing them only lowers it. With zeros or negatives mixed in, reach for prefix sums instead.

## No answer

Start `best` at an impossible value (n + 1, or infinity) and translate it at the end. Starting at 0 would make `min` return 0 every time.
lessons.commonMistakes:
- **Recording after the loop** (the longest-window habit). By then the window is invalid and too short.
- **Starting `best` at 0.** `min(0, …)` is always 0; use n + 1 or infinity for "not found".
- **Using `>` instead of `>=`** when the statement says "at least".
- **Applying it to arrays with negative numbers**, where removing an element can raise the sum.

lessons.title: Counting windows: every valid subarray
lessons.summary: For each right end, the valid starts form one unbroken range — add its size instead of listing subarrays.
objectives: Count all subarrays satisfying a monotone condition in O(n)
Explain why right − left + 1 new subarrays are valid at each step
Turn an "exactly K" count into two "at most" counts
lessons.concept:
Some questions ask **how many** subarrays satisfy a condition. Listing them is O(n²) or worse. With a monotone condition you can count them all in O(n).

Run the usual grow-and-shrink scan. After shrinking, `a[left..right]` is the **longest** valid window ending at `right`. Because the condition is monotone, every shorter window ending at `right` is valid as well — the ones starting at `left`, `left + 1`, …, `right`. That's `right − left + 1` subarrays.

```python
left = count = 0
product = 1
for right in range(n):
    product *= a[right]
    while product >= k and left <= right:
        product //= a[left]
        left += 1
    count += right - left + 1
```

Each subarray is counted exactly once — at its own right end.

## Exactly K

"Exactly K distinct values" isn't monotone: a window with exactly K can grow into one with K + 1 and not come back. But "at most K" is. So count

```text
exactly(K) = atMost(K) − atMost(K − 1)
```

Subarrays with fewer than K distinct values are counted by both and cancel; those with exactly K are counted only by the first.

## Watch the edge cases

With products, k can be 0 or 1: no product of positive integers is below 1, so the shrink loop must be able to empty the window completely (`left <= right`) and count 0.
lessons.commonMistakes:
- **Adding 1 per step.** Each right end contributes `right − left + 1` subarrays, not one.
- **Not allowing the window to empty.** With k <= 1 nothing is valid; without `left <= right` the loop divides past the window.
- **Counting "exactly K" directly with one window.** Use at-most(K) − at-most(K − 1).
- **Overflow.** Counts reach n(n + 1)/2, and products can grow before you shrink — use 64-bit integers in C++/Java.
